title: Med Spa Deferred Revenue: How to Book Packages, Memberships and Discounts
summary: Med spa deferred revenue with worked examples: how to book packages, membership dues, credits and member discounts so your P&L stops overstating profit.
body_markdown:
## What Deferred Revenue Means for a Med Spa


Deferred revenue is money a patient has paid you for treatments, credit or benefits you still owe them. It sits on the balance sheet as a liability and moves to revenue when you deliver the service. For a med spa, it covers prepaid packages, treatments a patient bought and banked for later, gift cards, account credit and some kinds of membership dues.


The idea is simple. The trouble is volume. A clinic that sells packages, memberships and gift cards at the same checkout may have dozens of patients carrying prepaid balances at once, each one earned on a different schedule. The accounting rule behind it is the revenue standard known as ASC 606, which ties revenue to delivering what the customer paid for. Deal advisors at[VMG Health](https://vmghealth.com/insights/blog/financial-due-diligence-in-the-med-spa-industry-key-considerations/) describe med spas as cash-pay businesses whose earnings can look more volatile than they really are, because of prepaid packages, memberships and gift card sales.


## Why a Cash-Basis P&L Overstates Profit in Busy Months


On a cash basis, every package sale counts as income the day the card is charged. That looks great in December and terrible in February, when patients are redeeming what they already paid for and new cash is slow. The profit you see in the busy month is partly money you have not earned yet.


The size of the gap scales with how much you sell up front. One bookkeeping firm that works with spas,[SpaLedger](https://spaledger.pages.dev/blog/deferred-revenue-med-spa) , models a clinic selling $15,000 of packages a month with 60% redeemed in the same month and estimates monthly profit overstated by about $6,000. Your numbers will differ, but the direction does not. Our guide to[seasonal cash flow planning for med spas](https://decodahealth.com/blog/med-spa-seasonal-cash-flow-planning) covers the other half of this problem: the cash you will need in the quiet months to deliver what you sold in the busy ones.


## Packages: Book the Cash as a Liability, Earn It Session by Session


A prepaid package goes to deferred revenue when it is sold, and each completed session moves its share to service revenue. Nothing about the patient's payment changes. Only the timing of when you call it earned does.


A worked example from[Beancount's med spa bookkeeping guide](https://beancount.io/blog/2026/07/16/med-spa-bookkeeping-deferred-revenue-packages-gift-cards-memberships-guide) uses a six-session laser package sold for $1,800, or $300 per session:


Event Debit Credit Liability left


Package sold Cash $1,800 Deferred revenue $1,800 $1,800


Session 1 delivered Deferred revenue $300 Laser revenue $300 $1,500


Session 2 delivered Deferred revenue $300 Laser revenue $300 $1,200


Sessions 3-6 delivered Deferred revenue $1,200 Laser revenue $1,200 $0


The harder part is what happens off the happy path. A patient who stops halfway, asks for a refund or converts the rest to credit changes the liability, and each of those moves needs its own entry. Our[med spa package refund policy guide](https://decodahealth.com/blog/med-spa-package-refund-policy) sets out the rules to write down before those requests arrive. Converting an unused package to account credit does not erase the liability. It moves it from the package to the patient's credit balance.


## Member Discounts on Prepaid Treatments Change the Per-Session Value


When a discount applies to a bundle of prepaid treatments, the discount belongs to every unit in the bundle, so each unit is earned at its discounted value. This is where reports and bookkeepers most often disagree, because the invoice lists items at full price and the discount sits on a separate line.


Take a pattern that reached our support team: three add-on treatments listed at $200 each, sold with a 15% membership discount, which is $90 off the $600 total. The member pays $510 and uses one treatment the same day.


Item At list price After discount


Three treatments bought $600 $510


Value per treatment $200 $170


One used: revenue earned $200 $170


Two banked: liability left $400 $340


The $400 figure the clinic saw was the remaining balance at list price. The correct liability is $340, and the visit earned $170. Spreading the discount this way is the default rule in the revenue standard:[PwC's revenue guide](https://viewpoint.pwc.com/dt/us/en/pwc/accounting_guides/revenue_from_contrac/revenue_from_contrac_US/chapter_5_allocating_US/54allocating_discoun_US.html) quotes ASC 606-10-32-36, which says an entity "shall allocate a discount proportionately to all performance obligations in the contract" unless narrow conditions point the whole discount at specific items. If you run several kinds of member pricing, our[med spa discount policy guide](https://decodahealth.com/blog/med-spa-discount-policy) covers how to keep them from stacking.


## Memberships Come in Three Shapes, and Each Books Differently


A membership's accounting depends on what the dues actually buy, not on what the plan is called. Most med spa programs fall into one of three shapes, and many plans mix two of them.


What the dues buy When the dues are earned What sits in the liability


Spendable account credit (each $99 renewal adds $99 to spend) When the patient spends the credit The unspent credit balance


Set treatments (a facial every quarter, say) As each included treatment is delivered The value of treatments owed but not yet given


Discounts or perks only Generally over the month the dues cover Usually nothing beyond the current period


The credit shape behaves like a rolling gift card. The treatment shape behaves like a slow package. The discount shape is closest to a subscription, and the discounts themselves show up later as lower prices on the services the member buys. Accounting firm[CLA](https://www.claconnect.com/en/resources/blogs/health-care/fundamentals-of-your-medspa-revenue-what-to-do-errors-to-fix) makes the same point for med spas: revenue should reflect the earned portion when a membership includes services and credits, and it recommends tracking collected versus earned recurring revenue as its own measure.


Mixed plans are common. A plan that adds monthly credit and also includes a periodic facial has two obligations, and your accountant will want to split the dues between them. The[membership pricing and retention guide](https://decodahealth.com/blog/med-spa-membership-pricing-retention) covers how to price those benefits; this section covers how they land on the books. Rolling credit with no expiry also grows without limit, which is the risk described in our post on[beauty banks and patient wallets](https://decodahealth.com/blog/setting-up-vip-memberships-beauty-banks-and-patient-wallets) .


## When You Change a Membership's Benefits, Change Its Accounting Too


If a membership used to grant account credit and you remove that credit, the way the plan's revenue is recognized has to change with it. Otherwise the system keeps holding each renewal back as if it were credit owed, even though no credit exists.


That is what one clinic's finance lead found. Its $99 monthly renewals were charging successfully, yet they appeared in neither revenue nor the patient credit liability report. The plan had originally been set up to grant a credit with every renewal, and its revenue setting was built around that. When the credit was removed, the setting stayed. Every renewal after that sat in limbo. The owner's answer made the intent clear: dues should create credit that stays a liability until the patient spends it, while the included facials (twice a year on one tier, quarterly on another) are a separate benefit.


Two habits prevent this:


- Write a one-line accounting rule next to every membership plan: what the dues buy and when they are earned.
- Treat any change to a plan's benefits as a finance change, too, and have whoever closes the books sign off before it goes live.


Plan changes rarely happen alone. If you are also raising dues, our guide to[raising med spa membership prices](https://decodahealth.com/blog/med-spa-membership-price-increase) covers the member communication side.


## Why a $0 Redemption Invoice Is Not Zero Revenue


When a patient uses a treatment they already paid for, the checkout invoice shows $0 due. That only means no new money changed hands. On an accrual view, the visit still earns the treatment's prepaid value.


This is the most common reason owners think revenue went missing. In the discount example above, a finance lead looked for the $170 on the revenue report and could not find it, because the report opened on a cash view by default. On a cash view, the full $510 counted on the day of purchase, so the later visit adds nothing. On an accrual view, the purchase adds $510 to the liability and the visit moves $170 into revenue.


Before you escalate a "missing revenue" question to your software vendor or bookkeeper, check two things: which basis the report is showing, and whether you are comparing an invoice's amount due with a revenue line. They answer different questions.


## Reconcile the Liability to Your Software Every Month


Once a month, compare the deferred revenue balance in your accounting system with the prepaid balances in your clinic software. They should match. When they do not, the gap almost always traces to something entered in one place and not the other.


1. Pull the outstanding balances from your clinic software: open packages, banked treatments, unspent account credit, unredeemed gift cards and unearned membership benefits.
2. Pull the deferred revenue accounts from your general ledger for the same date.
3. Investigate any difference. The usual causes are expired packages, refunds, comps, staff adjusting a banked quantity by hand, and patients imported from an old system.
4. Book the corrections and note what caused each one, so the same error is easier to spot next month.


Manual adjustments deserve their own line in the review. In the discount example, a hand edit to a banked quantity showed up as its own movement in the liability detail, which confused the review until someone traced it. If you recently switched systems, the[guide to what transfers in a med spa EMR migration](https://decodahealth.com/blog/med-spa-emr-migration-what-transfers) explains which balances need checking after import. For the wider month-end scorecard, see our[med spa KPI tracking guide](https://decodahealth.com/blog/med-spa-kpi-tracking) .


## What Deferred Revenue Means at Tax Time and When You Sell


Your tax method and your management reporting can differ. Many small practices file on the cash method, which the IRS allows for businesses that meet an inflation-indexed gross receipts test. For accrual-method taxpayers,[IRS Publication 538](https://www.irs.gov/publications/p538) allows advance payments to be postponed only until the next tax year, not beyond it. Ask your CPA which method applies to you before you change anything on your return.


The sale of a practice is where cash-basis books cost the most. Buyers and their advisors restate revenue to accrual during due diligence. VMG Health's review process includes unearned revenue reports and package and membership details, and it flags clinics that record package usage as write-offs or discounts instead of drawing down the prepaid balance. A clean, reconciled liability is far easier to defend than a pile of package sales booked as income.

## Final Thoughts on Med Spa Deferred Revenue


Most "missing revenue" questions we see are not missing revenue at all. They are a cash view read as accrual, a discount booked at list price, or a membership whose benefits changed while its accounting did not. Write one accounting rule per plan, spread discounts across what the patient bought, and reconcile the liability every month. Do those three and your P&L will show what you earned rather than what you collected. ## Frequently Asked Questions


Is a prepaid med spa package revenue when the patient pays?


Not under accrual accounting. The cash is yours, but the treatments are still owed, so the payment sits in a deferred revenue liability and moves to service revenue one session at a time as each treatment is delivered. Cash-basis books record the whole package as income on the day of sale, which is why a strong package month can make profit look far higher than the work you actually performed.


How do you account for a member discount on prepaid treatments?


Spread the discount across every unit the patient bought, then earn each unit at its discounted value. If three treatments listed at $200 each are sold for $510 after a $90 member discount, each one is worth $170, so one used treatment is $170 of revenue and two unused ones are a $340 liability. Booking the full list price per session overstates revenue on each visit.


How should a med spa book monthly membership dues?


It depends on what the dues buy. Dues that turn into spendable account credit stay a liability until the credit is spent. Dues that include set treatments are earned as those treatments are delivered. Dues that only unlock discounts or perks are usually earned over the month they cover. Write down which type each plan is, because the plan's benefits decide the accounting, not its name.


Why does my redemption invoice show $0 when the patient used a prepaid treatment?


A $0 redemption invoice means nothing more was owed at checkout because the patient paid earlier. It does not mean the visit earned nothing. On an accrual report, that visit moves the treatment's prepaid value out of the liability and into revenue. On a cash report, the money already counted on the day of purchase, so the visit adds nothing new.


Do med spas have to use accrual accounting?


Many small practices file taxes on the cash method, which the IRS allows for businesses under an inflation-indexed gross receipts threshold. Accrual reporting still matters for running the business, because it shows what you actually earned each month. Buyers, lenders and investors usually restate cash-basis med spa books to accrual during due diligence, so tracking deferred revenue now saves a painful cleanup later.


How often should a med spa reconcile its deferred revenue balance?


Monthly, at the same time you close the books. Compare the deferred revenue balance in your accounting system with the outstanding packages, banked treatments, unused credits and gift card balances in your clinic software. Any gap is usually an expired package, a refund, a manual adjustment or a comp that was entered in one system and not the other.
